ONE SENTENCE SUMMARY 30

Using a unique study design with temporally-dense, paired sampling of the oral cavity, nasal cavity 31

and oropharynx from the onset of naturally acquired human SARS-CoV-2 infection, we 32

demonstrate that Type I IFN responses are initiated synchronously in the upper respiratory mucosa 33

during early infection, whereas the timing of Type II IFN response initiation is asynchronous but 34

earlier initiation is associated with prior COVID-19 vaccination, enhanced tissue-resident memory 35

T cells signatures, and reduced local viral replication. 36

ABSTRACT 49

COVID-19 vaccines markedly reduce disease severity, but their ability to block infection and 50

transmission remains limited and variable.1 A better understanding of early mucosal 51

immune programs that constrain viral replication at susceptible upper respiratory sites is 52

needed to develop more effective antiviral strategies. However, temporal and anatomical 53

antiviral dynamics are difficult to resolve without longitudinal, paired-site sampling 54

beginning before infection onset. We quantified longitudinal viral load by RT-qPCR and 55

human gene expression by mRNA sequencing in 1,237 samples prospectively collected daily 56

from the nasal cavity, oral cavity, and oropharynx of 16 individuals starting from the onset 57

of naturally acquired SARS-CoV-2 infection, and 16 age-, sex-, and vaccination-matched 58

uninfected individuals. Here we show that Type I interferon (IFN) responses are initiated 59

concurrently across these upper respiratory sites, even before local viral detection. In 60

contrast, Type II IFN initiation is more spatially variable, and earlier nasal Type II IFN 61

initiation is associated with reduced viral replication, prior COVID-19 vaccination, and 62

higher tissue-resident memory T cell (TRM) signature expression. These findings demonstrate 63

that in addition to humoral immunity, prior vaccination primes rapid, inducible mucosal 64

Type II IFN responses, likely mediated by rare TRM upon viral encounter, to limit viral 65

replication and spread. 66

INTRODUCTION 68

Current COVID-19 vaccines provide robust protection against severe disease and can attenuate 69

breakthrough infection, but do not completely prevent onward transmission to new hosts.1,2 70

Transmission sustains opportunities for the emergence of variants that escape immunity conferred 71

by prior vaccination or infection.3 Vaccines that prevent onward transmission can interrupt this 72

cycle to reduce infection prevalence and the necessary scale of downstream infection control 73

measures.4 Understanding how early immune responses control viral replication at the primary site 74

of infection, the upper respiratory mucosa,5 is necessary to develop vaccines that limit 75

breakthrough infections, viral shedding and onward transmission.4 76

While considerable work has focused on optimizing antibody-mediated protection following 77

COVID-19 vaccination,6 early local mucosal immune responses that constrain viral replication 78

including interferon (IFN) responses have been relatively underinvestigated.7 The synchronization 79

of IFN response initiation among upper respiratory sites (e.g., nasal cavity, oral cavity, oropharynx, 80

nasopharynx) within an individual during early SARS-CoV-2 is unknown. Additionally, how the 81

timing of initiation for different IFN types (Type I, II, and III) at the onset of naturally acquired 82

SARS-CoV-2 infection in the upper respiratory mucosa of humans influences local viral 83

replication has not been demonstrated. It is also unclear whether prior COVID-19 vaccination 84

modulates the timing of IFN response initiation in the human upper respiratory mucosa during 85

breakthrough infection. 86

Available evidence suggests that the timing of IFN initiation is a key determinant of early viral 87

control.  Type I (IFN-α and IFN-β) and Type III IFNs (IFN-λ) are mostly produced by infected 88

cells after sensing viral pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMP), and signal through 89

interferon-stimulated gene factor 3 (ISGF3) complexes to elicit partially overlapping downstream 90

Obtaining longitudinal measurements of distinct IFN responses in upper respiratory 99

mucosal surfaces from the onset of SARS-CoV-2 infection in humans is logistically and 100

technically challenging. High frequency sample collection beginning before or at the onset of 101

infection is necessary to characterize how early upper respiratory mucosal immune responses 102

shape subsequent viral replication. Such samples have been obtained in controlled human viral 103

challenge studies, which typically involve experimentally inoculating a small cohort (<20 104

individuals) of young, healthy participants,15,16 as well as prospective cohort studies and case- 105

ascertained household transmission studies,14,17 though the onset of infection is observed in only a 106

small fraction of participants and sampling is typically less frequent or from a single upper 107

respiratory site. 108

household transmission study in the Los Angeles area between 2020-2022. Among over 400 111

participants, 16 were SARS-CoV-2–negative at enrollment but subsequently developed sustained 112

incident infection. These participants, together with 16 age-, sex-, and vaccination-matched 113

RESULTS 123

To interrogate early mucosal immune dynamics, we conducted a case-control study of 16 124

participants aged 7 to 57 years old with incident SARS-CoV-2 infection, as well as 16 age-, sex-, 125

and COVID-19 vaccination-matched uninfected controls (Table S1). We optimized methods to 126

overcome technical challenges inherent to self-collected human upper respiratory specimens, then 127

quantified longitudinal viral loads and performed human exome-enriched RNA sequencing on 128

1,273 specimens from paired upper respiratory mucosal sites (oral cavity, nasal cavity, 129

oropharynx) collected daily or twice daily by each participant (Figure 1, Figure S1). Following 130

RNA extraction, RT-qPCR analysis of a human housekeeping gene, MYH9, revealed only minor 131

sampling variation over time within each participant (Figure S2A-C). Successful cDNA libraries 132

were generated from 99% of all self-collected upper respiratory human clinical specimens 133

attempted (1262 of 1273, Figure S2D). Despite high microbial background, human exome 134

enrichment enabled greater than 10 million human mapping reads in over 90% of samples 135

attempted (1165 of 1273, Figure S2E) with high reproducibility among technical replicates 136

(Figure S2F-H). Gene expression data exhibited anticipated biological patterns by participant sex 137

and anatomical sampling site (Figure S2I,J). From this unique dataset, we investigated the relative 138

timing and synchronization of IFN responses among upper respiratory sites within SARS-CoV-2 139

infected individuals, how early IFN responses relate to viral loads throughout infection, and the 140

impact of prior COVID-19 vaccination. 141

Early Type I IFN responses were synchronized across the upper respiratory mucosa of 143

individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2, and often preceded viral detection in the nasal cavity 144

Since SARS-CoV-2 can infect multiple anatomical sites within the human upper 145

respiratory mucosa,20 early mucosal immune responses at each site and their coordination can 146

influence the course of infection. Therefore, we first sought to investigate the relationship between 147

timing of viral presentation and IFN responses. 148

Robust and well-validated gene sets were available for Type I and Type II IFN responses, 149

but not for Type III IFN responses. Published Type III IFN gene sets (GO:003434221 and 150

M3946422) were small (<15 genes) and dominated by IFNL transcripts, which at the bulk tissue 151

level were lowly expressed, resulting in gene set module scores that poorly differentiated infected 152

from uninfected participants (Figure S3). 153

Within infected individuals, SARS-CoV-2 presents in the nasal cavity several days after 154

the oral cavity or oropharynx.18,19 Among infected participants, detection of SARS-CoV-2 in the 155

nasal cavity occurred at least one day later than the oral cavity or oropharynx for 88% of 156

participants (Figure S1), on average, 2.3 days later. Aggregated trajectories demonstrate this 157

delayed rise in nasal cavity viral loads relative to the oral cavity and oropharynx (Figure 1A). 158

Given these differences in the timing of viral detection among upper respiratory mucosal sites, we 159

asked whether IFN responses were also asynchronous and followed local viral detection. 160

To our surprise, we found that initiation of the Type I IFN response did not always follow 161

the presence of viral RNA within a site, but initiated concurrently in the oropharynx, oral and nasal 162

cavities shortly after SARS-CoV-2 detection in any site. Canonical Type I IFN-inducible genes 163

(e.g., STAT2, MX1, MX2, OAS1, OAS2, IFIT1) exhibited low and stable expression among 164

uninfected participants, but dynamic rises in all upper respiratory anatomical sites from individuals 165

While concurrent initiation of the Type I IFN response was observed among upper 222

respiratory mucosal anatomic sites within infected individuals regardless of local viral detection, 223

Early initiation of Type II, but not Type I, IFN response was associated with reduced viral 237

replication 238

Understanding which immune responses effectively control viral replication and reduce 239

shedding in humans is crucial to designing vaccines that prevent breakthrough infections capable 240

of forward transmission. To investigate this, we next asked whether the timing of Type I or Type 241

II IFN responses within an upper respiratory site impacted subsequent viral replication from that 242

site. We used peak viral load (in RNA genomic copy equivalents per mL of sample) and the 243

integration of RNA viral load measurements over time (cumulative viral load) as indicators of viral 244

RNA shedding. 245

We analyzed longitudinal Type I and Type II IFN response module scores and viral loads 246

Pre-infection COVID-19 vaccination was associated with earlier Type II IFN responses and 287

reduced viral replication in the nasal cavity 288

We next asked whether prior COVID-19 vaccination was associated with earlier initiation 289

of IFN responses and reduced viral replication. Given that Type I IFN signaling is an innate 290

antiviral response, prior vaccination was neither expected nor observed to associate with earlier 291

Type I IFN response initiation in either the nasal or oral cavities (Figure 3A,B). 292

In contrast, prior COVID-19 vaccination was associated with earlier initiation of a Type II 293

IFN response in the nasal cavity (Figure 3A). Orthogonal analysis using a time-to-event 294

framework further demonstrated significantly earlier initiation of Type II but not Type I IFN 295

responses in the nasal cavities of vaccinated individuals (Figure S15E,F). Vaccination was also 296

associated with reduced cumulative viral replication in the nasal cavity (Figure 3B), and 297

significantly lower peak viral loads (Figure 3C). However, only 50% of individuals with prior 298

vaccination suppressed peak viral loads in the nasal cavity below 107 copies/mL (Figure S15G), 299

a presumably transmissible viral load.24 In the oral cavity, vaccination was not associated with 300

earlier Type I or Type II IFN responses, nor significantly reduced viral loads (Figure 3D-F). 301

DISCUSSION 410

Upper respiratory mucosal surfaces are the primary sites of respiratory viral infection, 411

replication and shedding, thus early immune responses that constrain viral replication at these sites 412

can reduce the risk of onward transmission. Using human gene expression measurements from a 413

unique set of paired samples from upper respiratory anatomical sites prospectively collected daily 414

by individuals who became infected with SARS-CoV-2, we characterized the timing and spatial 415

synchronization of early mucosal Type I and Type II IFN responses, their relative impacts on viral 416

replication, and their modulation by prior COVID-19 vaccination. 417

Despite differences in early viral load trajectories among the nasal cavity, oral cavity and 418

oropharynx of SARS-CoV-2 infected individuals, Type I IFN responses were initiated 419

concurrently and often preceded detectable viral RNA in the nasal cavity. This result supports that 420

testing for upregulation of nasal ISGs might enable earlier detection of viral infection to initiate 421

earlier treatment or infection control measures.32–35 Among unvaccinated participants with 422

sustained infection after SARS-CoV-2 challenge, ISGs were upregulated in the blood prior to the 423

nasal cavity, suggesting a potential systemic route for synchronization among upper respiratory 424

mucosal sites.15 425

Our analyses demonstrated that Type II IFN responses were not synchronized across upper 426

respiratory mucosal sites within infected individuals, but earlier initiation was associated with 427

lower local viral loads.  Moreover, earlier initiation of Type II IFN responses was observed among 428

participants with prior COVID-19 vaccination. Vaccinated individuals also exhibited subtle but 429

constitutively elevated expression of IFN-γ-inducible and TRM genes in the nasal cavity, which 430

were further upregulated shortly after viral infection. 431

Our results fortify the link between enrichment of upper respiratory TRMs, earlier initiation of 432

Type II IFN responses, and constraint of local viral replication in humans with naturally acquired 433

SARS-CoV-2 infection. TRMs have a recognized role in limiting viral replication,36–38 including by 434

rapidly producing IFN-γ upon SARS-CoV-2 exposure, as demonstrated  in ex vivo nasal mucosal 435

tissue39 and human lungs.25 In mice, airway CD4+ T cells recognizing SARS-CoV epitopes 436

induced rapid local IFN-γ production and reduced disease burden.40 In a trial of non-human 437

primates, IFN-γ induction by mucosal CD8+ T cells in the absence of SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing 438

antibodies (NAbs) yielded similar reductions in nasal viral load as Nab-inducing vaccines.41 In 439

human cross-sectional studies, higher magnitudes of a SARS-CoV-2-specific IFN-γ+ T cell 440

response in venous blood were associated with reduced risk of infection42 and the presence of IFN- 441

γ+ T cells in the upper airways was shown to prime viral recognition for enhanced viral clearance 442

and local control of SARS-CoV-2 replication.43 Longitudinal measurements from a SARS-CoV-2 443

human challenge study of unvaccinated individuals further support the role of T cells in local viral 444

clearance: CD4+ and CD8+ T cells infiltrated nasal mucosa within 1 day of inoculation for 9 445

participants with transient and abortive infections, but several days later among 7 participants with 446

sustained infection.15 Establishment of TRMs in the upper respiratory mucosa and early activation 447

of a Type II IFN response may constitute correlates of protection for vaccines intending to reduce 448

viral replication and forward transmission. 449

Several studies have demonstrated that intramuscular COVID-19 vaccination can elicit or 450

enhance early activation of TRM populations in upper respiratory mucosal sites,28,44–46 though 451

traditionally, intramuscular vaccines have not been very effective in establishing TRM in the 452

respiratory tract.28–30,40,47–49 Mucosal vaccines50 or hybrid strategies which follow intramuscular 453

vaccination with an intranasal adjuvant  (e.g. SARS-CoV-2 spike protein),51–55 have been shown 454

Design of a COVID-19 Household Transmission Study to Identify Individuals with Incident 499

As previously described,61 between September 2020 and March 2022, individuals aged 6 501

diagnosed with SARS-CoV-2 were eligible to participate in our case-ascertained COVID-19 503

household transmission study (approved by the California Institute of Technology IRB, protocol 504

#20-1026). Participants completed demographics and health questionnaires, as well as daily or 505

USA). These upper respiratory specimens underwent testing for SARS-CoV-2 viral RNA using 510

Statistical Analyses 546

For longitudinal analyses, time was represented either as days relative to study enrollment 547

(for uninfected participants) or to the first detectable SARS-CoV-2 RNA in any anatomical site 548

within each infected participant. Longitudinal trajectories (viral load, individual genes, or module 549

scores) were summarized within stated time windows by pooling available sample-level 550

observations after rounding time to the nearest day, with 95% confidence intervals estimated for 551

each window by percentile bootstrap with 1000 resamples. Samples with no detectable virus (ND) 552

were imputed to a value of 1 copies/mL, and samples with detectable but not quantifiable viral 553

loads (NQ) were imputed to a value of 10 copies/mL. Cumulative viral load was calculated using 554

trapezoidal integration of linear-scale viral load measurements from a given participant and 555

anatomical site, then log10-transformed for downstream analyses. Trapezoidal integration was 556

also applied to linear-scale, normalized gene expression measurements to calculate cumulative 557

gene expression within given infection windows, then log1p-transformed for downstream analyses. 558

Module scores for pre-defined gene sets representing relevant immune programs (Type I, 559

II, and III IFN, and tissue-resident memory T cells) were computed from the log1p-transformed 560

normalized bulk RNA-seq expression matrix using a control-gene-subtracted approach: for each 561

sample, the mean expression of genes in the target set was calculated and compared with the mean 562

expression of a pooled expression-matched control background. For each target gene, up to 1,000 563

control genes were randomly sampled without replacement from genes with mean expression 564

within 90-110% of the mean expression of the target gene. The mean expression of the pooled 565

sampled control genes was then subtracted from the mean expression of the target gene set to yield 566
